citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

The **countable choice principle** used throughout this pair, written
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the assertion:

> For every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a
> function $c$ with domain $\mathbb N$ such that $c(n)\in A_n$ for every
> $n\in\mathbb N$.

Here "sequence" means a function on $\mathbb N$ ([[def-function]]). We call
the displayed selector $c$ an **indexed choice function** for the sequence.
Its domain is the index set $\mathbb N$, whereas a choice function in
[[def-choice-function]] has as domain the family of sets themselves. These
notions must be distinguished when factors repeat. A family choice function
$g$ on $\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ gives an indexed selector by $c(n)=g(A_n)$;
the equivalence of the two existence assertions is explained in
[[def-countable-choice]].

This is the sequence formulation of countable choice. The equivalent
nonempty-product formulation, that $\prod_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ is nonempty for
every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets, is verified in
[[lem-countable-choice-sequence-and-product-formulations-are-equivalent]]; that
lemma is recorded as the well-definedness certificate of the present
definition.

In this pair $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is a stated hypothesis of the foliation
theorems and of the items whose proof selects countably many plaque data. It is
not assumed where a proof does not use it, and the items that consume it state
the hypothesis explicitly.

This pair-local carrier is retained deliberately: it restates the published
[[def-countable-choice]] in exactly the sequence form consumed by the
foliation items, and the published definition supplies the same principle. The
retention and its cross-batch consequences are recorded in the Step-3 report
of this pair (finding F4).

For every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets, there exists a
indexed choice function $c$ with domain $\mathbb N$ and $c(n)\in A_n$ for every
$n\in\mathbb N$ if and only if the product $\prod_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ is
nonempty. Thus the sequence formulation of
[[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]] and the nonempty-product
formulation of the same principle are equivalent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

derivations.claim: Take the round unknot $K\subset S^3$ with its standard oriented flat disk $F$ in a coordinate ball. The disk is connected, compact, and smooth, and its Euler characteristic is $1$, so [F1] gives genus $g=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(K,F)$ and $(K',F')$ be oriented knot and spanning-surface pairs in the oriented standard three-sphere, and let $h_t:S^3\to S^3$ be a smooth ambient isotopy with $h_0$ the identity, $h_1(K)=K'$, and $h_1(F)=F'$, preserving the given orientations. If $V$ and $V'$ are their Seifert matrices in any integral bases, then the basis transported by $h_1$ has matrix $V$, and any other target basis with transition matrix $P$ has matrix $V'=P^TVP$. Hence $V$ and $V'$ are S-equivalent, meaning they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two elementary rank-two enlargement moves or their reverses.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$
A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).
$$

derivations.claim: Under [A1], apply the Seifert-pairing convention to the source's supplied oriented surface and basis. In the original source basis, $A_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(f_i^-,f_j)$. By symmetry and a simultaneous positive normal translation, this equals $\operatorname{lk}(f_j^+,f_i)$, which is the $(j,i)$ entry of the positive-first matrix in the same basis. Thus that matrix is $A^T$. Let $S=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ be the basis swap. Then $S^TA^TS=A$, so the positive-first matrix in the swapped basis is the displayed $V$.

Direct multiplication gives $V-V^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Also $V-tV^T=\begin{pmatrix}1-t&t\\-1&1-t\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $(1-t)^2+t=1-t+t^2$. The skew-part identity agrees with the oriented genus-one handle intersection block in the stated positive-normal convention.

For $P_0$, $VP_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_0^T(VP_0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. For $P_1$, $VP_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_1^T(VP_1)=\begin{pmatrix}3&5\\4&7\end{pmatrix}$. Both determinants are $1$, so both are integral basis changes; the second matrix differs from $V$ in all four entries.

For either unimodular $P$, $(P^TVP)-t(P^TV^TP)=P^T(V-tV^T)P$. Right multiplication by $P$ does not change the image of the map on $\Lambda^2$, and left multiplication by the automorphism $P^T$ identifies the two cokernels. The module presentation is therefore independent of these basis changes, as asserted.
